planting.note: Do not attempt to transplant or purchase this species; it has no root system usable outside its native fungal network and digging it up is prohibited in most of the parks and forests where it grows. Appreciate it only in situ beneath mixed-conifer canopy as it pushes up through melting snowpack.

directions: Snow plant is a leafless, chlorophyll-free perennial of the Sierra Nevada and southern Cascade mixed-conifer belt that draws all of its nutrition from mycorrhizal fungi shared with overhead pines and firs rather than from sunlight. Its waxy, blood-red stalk and clustered bell flowers erupt through duff and receding snowbanks in late spring, often standing alone against bare soil before surrounding plants have leafed out. Because its survival depends entirely on an intact fungal network tied to mature conifer roots, it cannot be grown in a garden bed, propagated from seed, or safely moved, and should be treated strictly as a wild forest-floor spectacle to observe and photograph rather than cultivate. Leave plants undisturbed; picking or digging quickly kills them and removes a visible sign of a healthy underground fungal web.
sources: Yosemite National Park Service interpretive resources

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions or rooted cuttings in fall into well-drained duff or decomposed granite beneath pines; seed is rarely used since germination is slow and unreliable compared to vegetative starts.

directions: Mountain misery forms a dense, sprawling evergreen mat of finely divided, fern-like leaves across the forest floor of yellow-pine and mixed-conifer belts of the Sierra Nevada and southern Cascades, often carpeting entire slopes beneath open pine canopy. Every part of the plant is coated in a sticky, pungently resinous film that gives it its common name, discouraging browsing and making it a tough, low-maintenance groundcover once established. Small white, strawberry-like flowers appear in loose clusters in late spring, but the plant is grown chiefly for its fine aromatic texture and drought tolerance rather than bloom. Plant it on a dry slope under high, filtered shade where little else will thrive, and expect it to resprout vigorously from its woody rootstock after fire or hard pruning.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root stock or rooted hardwood cuttings in fall into moist, humus-rich soil along a shaded seep, streambank, or forest-edge planting; seed requires a cold, moist winter stratification and germinates erratically the following spring.

directions: Sierra currant is a lanky, arching deciduous shrub of streambanks and moist mixed-conifer understory through the Sierra Nevada, Cascades, and Klamath-Siskiyou ranges, where it leans into shaded seeps and creek margins that stay damp through summer. Drooping clusters of deep rose-pink flowers open in spring well before the maple-shaped leaves fully expand, drawing early hummingbirds and native bees, followed by blue-black berries with a dusty bloom that birds strip quickly. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich soil in dappled shade along a streamside planting, pond margin, or north-facing woodland edge, since it struggles where summer soil dries out completely. Older canes can be thinned at the base every few years to keep the arching form open and encourage fresh flowering wood.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings from container stock in fall so roots establish before summer drought; like most manzanitas it resents summer transplanting and benefits from sharp drainage and minimal soil disturbance.

directions: Pinemat manzanita hugs rocky, high-elevation ground beneath open red fir, lodgepole pine, and mountain hemlock stands of the Sierra Nevada and Cascade Range, forming a dense, ground-hugging mat rarely more than knee-high but spreading widely over gravelly slopes. Small clusters of white-to-pink urn-shaped flowers open in late spring, followed by small red-brown berries that persist into fall and feed birds and small mammals. It performs best in sharply drained, mineral soil under light, high-elevation forest shade, and resents heavy clay, summer irrigation, or deep mulch piled against the stems. Use it on a dry slope, rock garden, or beneath widely spaced pines as a long-lived, nearly maintenance-free evergreen groundcover once roots are established.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Set container-grown plants in fall into lean, rocky, well-drained soil beneath open conifer canopy; fresh nuts can be fall-sown after cold stratification but are slow and inconsistent compared to nursery transplants.

directions: Bush chinquapin is a tough, slow-growing evergreen shrub of rocky slopes and open conifer forest from the Sierra Nevada through the Cascade and Klamath ranges, usually found at the margins of pine and fir stands where light filters through rather than in deep shade or full exposure. Its leathery, dark green leaves have a distinctive golden-fuzzed underside, and in mid-to-late summer it produces spiny, chestnut-like burrs that split open in their second year to release small edible nuts favored by squirrels and jays. Plant it in lean, fast-draining, rocky or decomposed-granite soil at a woodland edge or on a dry bank, since it is intolerant of rich garden soil and summer irrigation. Growth is slow, so give it room to eventually form a broad mound and avoid heavy pruning, which it tolerates poorly.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Direct-sow fresh seed in fall so winter cold naturally breaks dormancy, or set small divisions in early spring into lean, well-drained soil beneath open pines; seedlings are slow the first year.

directions: Goosefoot violet is a small, tufted perennial of dry pine and fir forest openings across the Sierra Nevada, southern Cascades, and Great Basin ranges, named for the angular, lobed shape of its leaves, which are often purple-tinged on the underside. Bright yellow flowers marked with fine purple-brown veining and a dusky purple back appear low to the ground shortly after snowmelt, finishing bloom before the dry season sets in. It is best suited to a lean, gritty rock garden or trough that mimics open montane duff rather than a rich perennial border, and goes summer-dormant in hot, dry conditions much as it does in the wild. Give it excellent drainage and resist the urge to fertilize or overwater, since rich, wet soil quickly rots the shallow rootstock.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs or sow fresh seed in fall into deep, humus-rich soil beneath red fir or mixed-conifer canopy; seed-grown plants need several years to reach blooming size, so division of established clumps gives faster results.

directions: This higher-elevation fawn lily grows in red fir and mixed-conifer forest of the Sierra Nevada, southern Cascades, and Klamath-Siskiyou ranges, often blooming right at the edge of retreating snowbanks in a way lower-elevation fawn lilies rarely do. Unlike its mottled-leaved relatives, it typically carries plain green basal leaves, and its nodding white flowers age through the day to a deepening rose-purple with a bright yellow throat. It wants a cool, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil under conifers that stays moist through spring growth and dries predictably as the plant goes dormant in summer. Treat it as a patient long-term planting for a mountain or high-elevation woodland garden rather than an instant performer, and avoid disturbing the soil once bulbs are sited.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall at a shaded seep, streambank, or wet-meadow margin where soil stays saturated through summer; bulbs resent drying out even briefly during the growing season.

directions: Sierra tiger lily grows tall and slender from wet meadows, seeps, and streambanks within the Sierra Nevada and southern Cascade mixed-conifer belt, favoring the dappled light at a forest-and-meadow edge over deep shade or open exposure. Whorls of narrow leaves climb the stem to small, upward-facing to slightly nodding orange to yellow-orange flowers heavily spotted with maroon, opening in mid to late summer well after most spring bulbs have finished. Because it comes from consistently saturated mountain soil, it performs best in a bog garden, streamside bed, or irrigated woodland edge rather than a typical dry perennial border, and resents any extended drying of the root zone. Mulch lightly to keep roots cool and moist, and leave clumps undisturbed for years, since lily bulbs establish and multiply slowly but reward patience with increasing numbers of flowering stems.
